receipt.public_excerpt: Siemiatkowski said his company was able to stop hiring a year ago as it invested in artificial intelligence that’s doing the work of hundreds of staff across the firm.

evidence_items.explanation: Klarna's CEO publicly touted AI replacing hundreds of staff and a hiring freeze dating to 2023. This shows sustained public hype.

receipt.public_excerpt: an announcement in 2024 about how AI was doing the work of 700 customer service agents sent shares in call centre provider Teleperformance SE spiralling.

evidence_items.explanation: Klarna's early 2024 AI workforce claim was big enough to move a call-center company's stock. That marks it as a prominent early case.

receipt.public_excerpt: "As cost unfortunately seems to have been a too predominant evaluation factor when organising this, what you end up having is lower quality,” he said.

evidence_items.explanation: The CEO publicly admitted the AI cost push had lowered quality and said Klarna would invest in human support. That matches 'realized they had screwed up'.

receipt.public_excerpt: In a year’s time he expects the natural attrition rate of 20% to continue, taking the workforce down to about 2,500 from the current level of 3,000.

evidence_items.explanation: The walkback was partial. Klarna kept shrinking its workforce with AI even as it added human support.

receipt.public_excerpt: accounting for over 75% of all AI-related cuts reported since 2023

evidence_items.explanation: Most AI-attributed U.S. cuts came in 2025. Klarna's 2023–2024 claims predate that wave, which fits 'long before it was trendy'.

unresolved_gaps: No full list of firms that announced AI-driven cuts before Klarna (for example IBM's 2023 hiring pause), so 'among the first' is judged by prominence and timing, not exact rank.
No systematic comparison of when other firms reversed AI staffing moves.
